newsitem.title: COMOROS: Airline makes plans to repatriate plane crash dead.
newsitem.headline: Airline makes plans to repatriate plane crash dead.

text.p: A lack of coffins on the Moslem Comoro Islands is hindering efforts to repatriate the bodies recovered from an Ethiopian Airlines plane that crashed there, a senior police official said on Monday.

"The problem we have is that we have no coffins in the Comoros. We are a Moslem country. Possibly Ethiopian Airlines may bring some in," the Commander of the Comoran gendarmerie, Ismael Mognidaho, told Reuters.
Moslems bury their dead in shrouds instead of coffins and cremation is not allowed.
He said the authorities of the islands, lying in the Indian Ocean 300 km (190 miles) east of the African mainland, had no problem in principle with a mass repatriation of the victims.
India's honorary consul in the Comoros had asked if Hindus could be cremated immediately, in line with the religion, but the request had been turned down.
"No, this is a Moslem country, that is desecration," Mognidaho said. "We could not allow this."
Ethiopian Airlines said it would transport all the bodies of the victims to Addis Ababa as soon as rescue efforts were completed.
It believes it will be easier for relatives to go to the Ethiopian capital than to the Comoros to identify their kin and make arrangements for the bodies.

Lia Belai, the public relations head of the airline, said that after proper identifications and prayer services in Addis Ababa, the bodies would be transported to their respective destinations accompanied by airline officials.
She said the airline would make arrangements for those who wished to take the body of a relative direct from the Comoros.

Of the 163 passengers and 12 crew on board the plane that was hijacked en route to Nairobi and West Africa from Addis Ababa, 145 were international travellers from some 35 countries and thirty were Ethiopians.
Fifty-two people survived. The rest are dead or presumed dead. Police said on Monday that around 40 bodies had still to be recovered from the wreckage.

The bodies that have been found are being kept in a makeshift morgue in what used to be the cold storage facilities of a meat importer. By early Monday only two families had arrived on the island to try to identify relatives.
Ethiopian Airlines said it would not be issuing a passenger list "until proper identifications were carried out and the next of kin was informed", Lia said.
Ethiopia has declared a three-day mourning period starting on Monday and flags are flying at half-mast.
The national radio played solemn music and the Ethiopian Orthodox Chruch said it would hold a requiem mass on Tuesday for all those who died in the crash.

The United States Embassy in Addis Ababa condemned what it called the "criminal and terrorist act" and said the Federal Bureau of Investigation would enter the investigation because U.S. citizens had been on the flight.
